title: Sample Flashcards (Evidence)
description: Eight sample cards on relevance, 403, and hearsay, using every cards/v1 field. Flip each card, shuffle the deck, remove the cards you know, and see them all at once under All cards.
source: Evidence Rules Outline, Parts I and V

cards.back: Evidence is relevant if both (all required):
points: (a) it has any tendency to make a fact more or less probable than it would be without the evidence (probativeness); and
(b) the fact is of consequence in determining the action (materiality).
cards.note: At trial, "irrelevant" covers both probativeness and materiality.

cards.back: Yes, unless the Constitution, a federal statute, the FRE, or other Supreme Court rules provide otherwise. Irrelevant evidence is not admissible.

cards.front: When relevance depends on whether a fact exists, how much proof of that fact is needed, and who decides?
cards.back: Proof sufficient to support a finding that the fact exists. The judge asks only whether a jury could reasonably find the fact by a preponderance (Huddleston), without weighing credibility; the jury decides.
cards.note: Contrast 104(a): the judge herself decides by a preponderance, not bound by the evidence rules except privilege.

cards.front: When may the court exclude relevant evidence under Rule 403?
cards.back: When its probative value is substantially outweighed by a danger of (any one suffices):
cards.note: The rule tilts toward admission: exclusion only when the imbalance is substantial.

cards.front: What factors does a court weigh in the 403 balance?
points: (1) whether the fact is actually disputed;
(2) the availability of other means of proof; and
(3) the likely effectiveness of a limiting instruction.

cards.front: What is a "statement" for hearsay purposes?
cards.back: A person's oral assertion, written assertion, or nonverbal conduct, if the person intended it as an assertion.

points: (1) the declarant does not make while testifying at the current trial or hearing; and
(2) a party offers to prove the truth of the matter asserted.
cards.note: You can't say whether something is hearsay without knowing the proponent's purpose.

cards.front: Name four kinds of out-of-court words or conduct that are not hearsay.
points: Words offered for their effect on the listener (notice, motive, reasonable fear).
Words offered as circumstantial evidence of knowledge.
